H1.text: Five friends. Two badges. One says captain. The other says vice captain.

H2.text: How many ways can the two badges be given out? Most people guess ten. The real answer is twenty.

H3.text: Diya watched this happen at her class election today.

H4.text: Meera as captain, Sana as vice. Or Sana as captain, Meera as vice. Same two girls. So why count them twice?

H5.text: Because the two badges are different. When the order matters, we are counting permutations.

P2.text: Picture a row of chairs, and each chair has its own label. First chair. Second chair.

P3.text: A permutation is an arrangement in a definite order of a number of objects, taken some or all at a time.

P4.text: Arrangement means putting things into places. Definite order means the first place and the second place are not the same.

P5.text: Some or all at a time means we may fill only a few places, or every place.

K1.text: Side by side. Meera is captain, Sana is vice captain. Now swap the badges.

K2.text: Same two people, but each one has a different job. So these are two different arrangements.

K3.text: Now a team of two, with no badges. Meera and Sana is the same team as Sana and Meera. There, order does not matter.

K4.text: Now you try. A lock code one, two, three, and a lock code three, two, one. Same, or different? Pause and decide.

K5.text: Different! The lock opens only in the right order. So a lock code is a permutation.

L1.text: Now let us count every way, one square at a time.

L2.text: Write the five friends down the side. These are the captains.

L3.text: Write them again across the top. These are the vice captains.

L4.text: Each square is one pair. Ravi captain, Meera vice is one square.

L5.text: But one person cannot wear both badges. So the squares on this diagonal are crossed out.

L6.text: Five rows, and four good squares in each row. Five times four. Twenty ways, not ten.

D1.text: Now the shortcut, with no squares at all.

D2.text: Think of two empty places. The first place is captain. Any of the five friends can take it. Five choices.

D3.text: The second place is vice captain. One friend is already used up. So four choices are left.

D4.text: The fundamental principle of counting says: multiply the choices. Five times four is twenty.

D5.text: Now make it general. Say we have n different things, and r places to fill.

D6.text: The first place has n choices. The second has n minus one. The third has n minus two.

D7.text: Each place uses up one thing. So the last place, place number r, has n minus r plus one choices.

D8.text: Multiply them all. This product is written n P r. The P stands for permutation.

V1.text: Watch it grow. Keep five friends, and add one place at a time.

V2.text: One place, five ways. Two places, twenty. Three places, sixty.

V3.text: Four places, one hundred and twenty. Five places, still one hundred and twenty.

V4.text: Quick one. Why did the count stop growing at the last place? Pause and think.

V5.text: When four places are filled, only one friend is left. One choice. And times one changes nothing.

G1.text: There is a neater way to write n P r. It uses factorials.

G2.text: n factorial means n times every whole number below it, down to one. Five factorial is one hundred and twenty.

G3.text: Our product stops early, at n minus r plus one. The part that is missing is n minus r factorial.

G4.text: So we divide it away. n P r equals n factorial, over n minus r factorial.

G5.text: Check it. Five P two is one hundred and twenty over three factorial, which is six. That gives twenty.

T1.text: Remember this. When order matters, n P r counts the ways to fill r places from n different things.

W2.text: Eight runners race. Gold, silver and bronze go to the first three. In how many ways can the medals be given?

W3.text: Step one. Gold is not the same as silver, so order matters. This is a permutation.

W4.text: Step two. n is eight runners. r is three medals.

W5.text: Step three. Eight P three is eight factorial over five factorial.

W6.text: Step four. Everything from five down cancels, leaving eight times seven times six.

W7.text: So there are three hundred and thirty six ways.

X2.text: Many students write eight times eight times eight. That is five hundred and twelve.

X3.text: But one runner cannot win two medals. The rule n to the power r is only for when repeats are allowed. Here, it is eight times seven times six.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main, as questions that build numbers from given digits, with no digit repeated.

Q1.text: Exam level now. How many four digit even numbers can be made from these six digits, with no repeats? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. One hundred and fifty six.

A2.text: Even means the last digit is zero, two or four. Put zero last. The other three places take five, four and three choices. That is sixty.

A3.text: Now put two or four last. That is two choices.

A4.text: The first digit cannot be zero, and cannot be the last digit. Four choices. The middle two take four and three. Two times four times twelve is ninety six.

A5.text: Sixty plus ninety six is one hundred and fifty six.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why are Meera captain, Sana vice, and Sana captain, Meera vice, two different ways?

Y4.text: Three. Why is five P four equal to five P five?

N1.text: Next time: the word APPLE has two P's. Swap them, and nothing changes. So how many different words can APPLE really make?
